I got a little caught up on that, too. I don't think it's actually a contradiction, just that it could be perhaps explained differently. Consider:

- If the newspaper article had said "David Sotheby is 70 years old." in 1982, then after David took a pill, it would be a 1982 article reading "David Sotheby is 69 years old." But this only applies for an article that actually lists the subject's age.

- If the newspaper article had said "David Sotheby won the local Fun Run" in 1982, then nothing about taking the pills would change any of that. The only discrepancy here would be that, knowing David in 2015, you should be able to deduce that he is at minimum 33, regardless of how many pills were taken.

How plausible that scenario really is is kind of problematic, but that's my reading on its execution.

item.content:encoded:
Oh wow, I'm really late to this discussion.

+ show block
– hide block

Yeah, SCP-483 could definitely use some tweaks in tone, and I agree with many of your points. As the author, I'd love to give it a bit of TLC, perhaps add a couple of interviews with affected individuals to clarify the weird age dissonance in the minds of people around them… However, I can't rely on myself to find time to participate in the discussion, as you can see by how late this message is coming for instance. Feel free to let people suggest and implement changes to the SCP without requiring my input. (I might come in and add something myself, but I might not.)

As long as multiple people are discussing it instead of moving unilaterally, like a couple people in the SCP IRC for instance, it's fine by me. It's my experience that when more than one site member collaborates on something, even on small changes, the page turns out better no matter who was doing the discussing. I can trust that, even if the author (me) isn't involved.

While I'm here, though, I guess I'll address some of the discrepancies you're concerned about re. the nature of this SCP and its effects:

For example, wouldn't people realize something wrong since they insist their friend is younger than he actually is when the article suggests they should still be able to remember for how long they've known each other, when they've celebrated birthday parties, etc? Wouldn't they find it odd that their supposedly pre-teen friend is clearly an adult, has a job and everything?

Yes, they would realize something is wrong, when pressed — and they do, as well. All they are is convinced that (1) the affected person is X years old, (2) that their date of birth is Y to match, (3) that said individual was X-Z years old when something Z years ago happened, such as if it was the individual's X-Zth birthday, and (4) that for all the years they've known the individual, the idea that they're that age never struck them as odd.

Sure, they might take a fresh look at Fred and quietly think, "I can't believe he's only fifteen years old". However, it'll be difficult for them to question it that much if they've known Fred for long, because if they're close enough to him to care about the issue, they might remember having known Fred for upwards of five or ten years without the "I can't believe he's so young" thought ever having struck them. This causes a nice psychological effect, doesn't it? "If I really thought it was this odd for Fred to be so young, then why didn't I question it for the previous five years? I must be imagining things." And then the confusing thought gets dismissed… or possibly compounded, if they check with official documents and find that the especially-young age is corroborated everywhere, or if Fred takes so many pills that people think they remember events twenty years ago that involved him.

Imagine hiring Fred for a line of work, supervising him for five years, then looking at the tax documents you're about to give him for the new year and realizing — inexplicably and belatedly — that he's not old enough to legally work. And not only he's not old enough… that you knew he wasn't old enough, hired him anyway, and have been putting his underage status on your company's tax forms for five years without once realizing that what you were doing was illegal. How screwed are you? How will you react to realizing this, how do you avoid fines and jail time, and what in god's name do you do with Fred now?

Toward the end of the description, the article mentions that "Affected individuals may be convinced that their interpretation of the subject's age is wrong and revise it," meaning that it IS possible to confront someone with the idea that they were clearly participating in an event with Fred twenty years ago, and so Fred must really be over twenty in age. They'll believe it, if you present them with enough proof. The mental dissonance is a feature, not a bug… imagine running into such a situation in your own life, and how it might make you question your sanity, especially since your thoughts are NOT being actively edited by anything. A single, broad change to your memories, and then the rest is left for your psyche to sort out on its own.

I will grant you this, though: This concept is very poorly explored in the article as-is. One of the most effective ways I can imagine to improve this article would be to add in a few interviews with family members and acquaintances of those who have ingested the SCP, showing just how oddly these memory-edits manifest and how different people reconcile them. Unlike many other SCPs of the memory- and perception-altering variety, this one DOESN'T force people to shut down or go into seizures when they fail to reconcile their false memories with reality, or their real memories with age-adjusted documents. It's up to the individual to realize (or not realize) that there's such a discrepancy between their perception, reality, and the truth, and up to the individual to decide how to react to this fact in (quite likely) a variety of ways.

This is part of why I made the decision to have Subject Zero killed. This SCP, point-blank, WILL cause some civilians to ask questions and put together that there's been an inexplicable supernatural occurrence, and leaves an extensive paper trail due to the oddly flawed nature of its incredibly specific and broad edits. You can put together, from newspapers alone, the indisputable fact that an impossible number of historical documents have been genuinely altered with a specific purpose in mind! The easiest way to quell further questions on the issue is to "undo" as many of the document edits as you can to remove historical discrepancies, and then kill the person whose memories and existence are by far the most likely to highlight them or invoke the question in others.

As for this bit of mine:

…since "If SCP-483-1 is ingested in a quantity greater than an organism's original age, the organism loses all memory aside from functional memory", how does Dr. Blast remember working for the SCP Foundation in the past, what his status there used to be and the incident that lead him to lose his position? Why would he still work for the Foundation if nobody knows who he is and his diplomas are gone? Why is no-one in the Foundation questioning the hiring of a two-weeks-old adult?

This is a little looser; I wasn't entirely playing by the rules, and some of this is listed in Dr. Blast's personnel file rather than here. You see a bit in the article, though, with this sentence: "Lucky for me, my countermeasures saved my memory from the overdose."

Basically, I implied that Dr. Blast — possibly while working with another SCP, or perhaps due to extreme latent paranoia — had devised a method to back-up and preserve his true memories somewhere SCP-483's edits cannot reach, in a way which automatically restored them at some point after 483 wiped him clean. Or at least, Dr. Blast alleges this. There might not be any official record on how he preserved his memories in a way which evades 483's reach; Dr. Blast might not have divulged it, might have divulged a story with discrepancies, or his story is unverifiable. Other than his (few) personal merits and knowledge, there may be no way to confirm he ever worked at the Foundation for certain, and perhaps he never actually had. However, by some stroke of luck — or perhaps by proving annoying, harmless, and just useful enough to make further scrutiny worthwhile — he's been assigned to Safe-class research work "again", and is almost certainly never going to be allowed around anything dangerous or important.

It's a little cheesy, sure. I suppose I felt a bit too green to write myself a self-insert doctor who had any sort of proven tenure.

Collapsed the wall of text. ~Zyn

item.content:encoded:
I must say I don't really like it. It feels like one of those articles that has potential but whose concept isn't developed very well, especially in light of the many holes and contradictions in the depiction of the effects.

For example, wouldn't people realize something wrong since they insist their friend is younger than he actually is when the article suggests they should still be able to remember for how long they've known each other, when they've celebrated birthday parties, etc? Wouldn't they find it odd that their supposedly pre-teen friend is clearly an adult, has a job and everything? Regarding the second addendum, how is it possible that anyone realizes they've forgotten someone if they have no mean of being reminded of them and apparently, even that person doesn't remember their own past?

And then there's the tonal issues. First, it's stated that the person who first owned the bottle was terminated… why? What does the Foundation gain from this aside from having to cover it up? Apparently no-one was finding anything weird with the discrepancies in the guy's life story so wouldn't it make more sense to leave him be? How was he in any way a threat? Shouldn't he have been kept as a potential SCP? It really comes across as one of those "the SCP Foundation really loves to kill civilians for no reason" moments which always bother me.

As for the comedy stuff, honestly, I don't mind "lolfoundation" or more comedic elements or notes (as long as they remain somewhat consistent with the rest of the article) but since "If SCP-483-1 is ingested in a quantity greater than an organism's original age, the organism loses all memory aside from functional memory", how does Dr. Blast remember working for the SCP Foundation in the past, what his status there used to be and the incident that lead him to lose his position? Why would he still work for the Foundation if nobody knows who he is and his diplomas are gone? Why is no-one in the Foundation questioning the hiring of a two-weeks-old adult?

Again, the idea has potential but it'd need a very heavy rewrite to be a good article.
